lessons.title: Constituents and hierarchy

outcomes.text: Find a constituent by tracing all and only its words to one node.

lessons.reviewed_by: Codex — scoped AI source review; not human instructor sign-off

teaching.text: A phrase marker records grouping, not just word order. A node dominates the elements below it; immediate domination has no intervening node. A sequence is represented as a constituent when a single node dominates exactly that sequence. At this stage, use phrase labels rather than later category labels.

worked_example.origin: Original SynTutor example applying the cited convention; not a copied book exercise or a parser prediction.

steps.text: Trace the words under PHRASE-b.
Notice that PHRASE-a also includes near.
Keep each word in one immediate grouping.

source.review_note: Original instructional example source-checked against cited B-R conventions; not a printed diagram.

lessons.title: Subject, predicate and category

outcomes.text: Identify subject and predicate from the immediate NP/VP split under S.

lessons.reviewed_by: Codex — scoped AI source review; not human instructor sign-off

teaching.text: Category labels and functions answer different questions. In the basic pattern S → NP VP, the NP immediately under S functions as subject, and its VP sister functions as predicate. Subject and predicate are functions derived from position, not extra phrase-marker nodes. Triangles leave internal structure unanalyzed.

worked_example.origin: Original SynTutor example applying the cited convention; not a copied book exercise or a parser prediction.

steps.text: Place S over the whole sentence.
Group The robins as the subject NP.
Make sing the VP sister of that NP.

source.review_note: Original instructional example source-checked against cited B-R conventions; not a printed diagram.

cambridge_insights.text: Cambridge distinguishes the sentence as a text-level unit from the clause as a syntactic category. Central clauses have a subject–predicate structure and clauses can be embedded. These terms provide grammatical context; they do not rename B-R S nodes. This classification is a teaching insight, not a whole-sentence correctness test.

options.feedback: The subject branch is NP in this V2 pattern.
Try again. Choose the category used at Chapter 2.
Try again. Choose the category used at Chapter 2.

guided.hint: Choose the category used at Chapter 2.

options.feedback: Try again. Follow the VP branch, not the subject NP.
Try again. Follow the VP branch, not the subject NP.
The VP immediately under S is the predicate.

transfer.hint: Follow the VP branch, not the subject NP.

options.feedback: Try again. Read the relation to S.

lessons.title: Heads and adjective phrases

outcomes.text: Identify an adjective head and represent a degree expression with AP, DEG and A.

lessons.reviewed_by: Codex — scoped AI source review; not human instructor sign-off

teaching.text: A phrase takes its category from its head. In this simple adjective phrase, the adjective is the head A and the preceding degree word is DEG. The phrase label is AP. A single adjective can also form an AP. Chapter 3 introduces these categories; it does not yet introduce NOM inside NP.

lessons.title: The basic transitive VP

outcomes.text: Represent a transitive verb and its direct-object NP as sisters inside VP.

lessons.reviewed_by: Codex — scoped AI source review; not human instructor sign-off

teaching.text: Chapter 4 distinguishes lexical-verb subcategories by their complements. In the transitive pattern, V carries [trans] and its NP complement is its sister under VP. That NP functions as direct object. The subject NP is outside VP. This lesson practices this pattern, not every possible use of every verb.

Place inspected under V [trans].
Attach the bridge as NP sister of V under VP.

lessons.title: Adjuncts and two levels of VP

outcomes.text: Distinguish a VP adjunct from a lexical verb complement by attachment.

lessons.reviewed_by: Codex — scoped AI source review; not human instructor sign-off

teaching.text: In the adopted Chapter 5 analysis, a verb complement is sister of V; an adjunct adverbial is sister of VP. A transitive V and its direct object form the inner VP. An optional adjunct can modify that VP to form a larger VP. Similar word sequences can have different attachments with different verbs; word order alone is insufficient.

worked_example.sentence: Nora inspected the bridge in June
worked_example.origin: Original SynTutor example applying the cited convention; not a copied book exercise or a parser prediction.

steps.text: Build the transitive inner VP inspected the bridge.
Keep in June together as PP.
Join that adjunct PP to the inner VP under an outer VP.

source.review_note: Original instructional example source-checked against cited B-R conventions; not a printed diagram.

lessons.title: Auxiliaries head their own VPs

outcomes.text: Represent a progressive auxiliary as head of a VP taking another VP as complement.

lessons.reviewed_by: Codex — scoped AI source review; not human instructor sign-off

teaching.text: The lexical verb and its complement still form a VP when an auxiliary precedes them. Each auxiliary heads its own VP and takes a VP complement. For this progressive example, is is PROG [pres], and inspecting the bridge is the lower VP. An auxiliary is not an adjunct just because it is sister of VP.

worked_example.origin: Original SynTutor example applying the cited convention; not a copied book exercise or a parser prediction.

steps.text: Build inspecting the bridge as the lexical VP.
Place is under PROG [pres].
Join PROG and its VP complement under the higher VP.

options.text: No, it takes a VP complement

options.feedback: Is is the progressive auxiliary, represented by PROG [pres].

lessons.title: DET and NOM inside NP

outcomes.text: Build the Chapter 7 core NP pattern with DET and NOM.

lessons.reviewed_by: Codex — scoped AI source review; not human instructor sign-off

teaching.text: Chapter 7 refines ordinary determiner-plus-noun phrases into NP → DET NOM. NOM is an intermediate level between NP and N. In the simple core pattern here, NOM contains N; DET contains the demonstrative DEM. Use this chapter’s core profile without the optional Appendix extra-NOM refinement. This pattern is not a demand that names and pronouns have overt determiners.

worked_example.origin: Original SynTutor example applying the cited convention; not a copied book exercise or a parser prediction.

steps.text: Put lanterns under N.
Make that N the child of NOM.
Put those under DEM and DET; join DET and NOM under NP.

lessons.title: Complementisers and subordinate clauses

outcomes.text: Represent an overt that-complementiser with C and S under S-bar.

lessons.reviewed_by: Codex — scoped AI source review; not human instructor sign-off

teaching.text: In the Chapter 8 that-clause pattern, the complementiser occupies C, which is daughter of S-bar and sister of S. The S below it contains the subject–predicate structure. Write S-bar in stored data and read it as S′. This lesson studies this overt that-clause pattern; it does not turn a chapter simplification into a universal rule for all subordinate clauses.

worked_example.sentence: that Nora is inspecting the bridge
worked_example.origin: Original SynTutor example applying the cited convention; not a copied book exercise or a parser prediction.

steps.text: Keep the complementiser that outside the lower S triangle.
Place that under C.
Join C and S under S-bar.

Central clauses have a subject–predicate structure and clauses can be embedded. These terms provide grammatical context; they do not rename B-R S nodes. This classification is a teaching insight, not a whole-sentence correctness test.

outcomes.text: Distinguish the C2 wh position from C1 and retain an NP gap for a fronted object.

lessons.reviewed_by: Codex — scoped AI source review; not human instructor sign-off

teaching.text: Chapter 9 adds S-double-bar (stored S-dbar) and separates C2 above C1. In the object wh-question demonstrated here, what occupies C2 and is occupies C1. lessons.title: The non-finite to-infinitive VP

outcomes.text: Represent infinitival to as a [-tense] auxiliary with a lexical VP complement.

lessons.reviewed_by: Codex — scoped AI source review; not human instructor sign-off

teaching.text: In the adopted Chapter 10 analysis, infinitival to is a [-tense] auxiliary, followed by a VP with a stem-form lexical verb. It is different from the preposition to in a place expression. The worked fragment here shows only the non-finite VP, so it makes no claim about an unshown subject controller. Do not infer a finite tense from the surface stem alone.

lessons.title: From sentence lists to grammars

outcomes.text: Explain why a finite set of rules can describe an unbounded set of sentences.

lessons.reviewed_by: Codex — scoped AI source review; not human instructor sign-off

teaching.text: Chapter 11 closes the course without adding a new tree profile. A finite inventory of remembered sentences cannot capture the open-ended possibilities of a natural language. Rules can describe how complex sentences are constructed and make predictions beyond already listed examples. The chapter’s ideal grammar both admits sentences and supplies their structural descriptions; a drawn tree alone is not a full grammar.

worked_example.sentence: Iris rests. / Leo waits. / Iris rests and Leo waits.
worked_example.origin: Original SynTutor example applying the cited convention; not a copied book exercise or a parser prediction.

steps.text: Start with two independently available sentences.
Combine them with and.
Notice that the same combination procedure can apply again.

lessons.title: Sentences and embedded clauses

outcomes.text: Distinguish a text-level sentence from a central subject–predicate clause that can be embedded.

lessons.reviewed_by: Codex — scoped AI source review; not human instructor sign-off

teaching.text: Cambridge distinguishes the sentence as a text-level unit from the clause as a syntactic category. Central clauses have a subject–predicate structure and clauses can be embedded. These terms provide grammatical context; they do not rename B-R S nodes. This classification is a teaching insight, not a whole-sentence correctness test.

worked_example.sentence: Nora reports that the robins sing.
worked_example.origin: Original SynTutor contrast; no new Cambridge tree labels are imposed on B-R.

steps.text: Read the whole utterance as one sentence in this text.
Locate the embedded clause the robins sing.
Notice its subject–predicate structure without treating it as a separate text sentence.
